title: Patching Array
statement:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers in non-decreasing order and an integer `n`. You may insert extra positive integers of your choice into the array; each inserted number is called a patch.

Afterwards, every whole number from `1` to `n` (both included) must be obtainable as the sum of some subset of the array's elements, where each element is used at most once (equal values at different positions are separate elements). Return the smallest number of patches that makes this true.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
notes:
## Intuition

Suppose every number from 1 to `reach` can already be built. Adding a value `x` with `x <= reach + 1` extends that to every number up to `reach + x`: the old sums still work, and `x` plus an old sum fills the rest. If the next array value is bigger than `reach + 1`, nothing can ever build `reach + 1` (the remaining values are even bigger), so a patch is forced. The best patch is `reach + 1` itself, the largest value that still leaves no gap, which roughly doubles `reach`. Trying every set of patches would explode; this greedy needs only one pass.

## Approach

1. Start with `reach = 0` (nothing is buildable yet), `patches = 0` and `i = 0`.
2. While `reach < n`:
   - if `nums[i]` exists and is at most `reach + 1`, use it: `reach += nums[i]` and move `i` on;
   - otherwise patch with `reach + 1`: `reach` becomes `2 * reach + 1` and `patches` grows by one.
3. Return `patches`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 3]`, `n = 6`.

- `reach = 0`: `nums[0] = 1 <= 1`, so `reach = 1`.
- `reach = 1`: `nums[1] = 3 > 2`, so patch 2: `reach = 3`, `patches = 1`.
- `reach = 3`: `nums[1] = 3 <= 4`, so `reach = 6`.
- `reach = 6` is not below `n`, so the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m + log n) for m array values: each step either consumes a value or at least doubles `reach`.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- In Java or C, `reach` can pass 2^31 - 1 before the loop stops; keep it in a 64-bit type.
- The test is `nums[i] <= reach + 1`, not `< reach + 1`: a value equal to `reach + 1` closes the gap exactly.
- Duplicates are separate elements, so `[1, 1, 1, 1]` builds every number up to 4.
- Values larger than `n` need no special case: while `reach < n` they always fail the `nums[i] <= reach + 1` test.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `reach` | every number from 1 to `reach` can be built so far |
| `patches` | how many numbers have been inserted |
| `i` | index of the next array value not yet used |

narration.2: Nothing can be built yet: the buildable range 1..reach is empty.
narration.3: No patches have been added so far.
narration.4: i points at the smallest array value not yet used.
narration.6: Keep going until every number up to n can be built.
narration.7: The next array value fits if it does not leave a gap after reach.
narration.8: Using it extends the buildable range by its value.
narration.9: Move on to the next array value.
narration.11: The next value is too big (or there is none), so reach + 1 is unreachable: patch it, which doubles the range.
narration.15: The whole range 1..n is covered; return the number of patches used.
